lead: A process is reversible only if it can be run backwards and leave absolutely no trace — in the gas, in the cylinder, in the room. Real engines never manage this, but the idea earns its place: it marks the best that any device could ever do between the same two states, so the gap between it and a real machine measures what we are wasting. This chapter defines the reversible process, lists what spoils it, and shows how the same gas expanding the same way can deliver work or deliver nothing.
prereq: You need: quasi-static process and path from Unit 1 (Unit 1), and the isothermal process of an ideal gas from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A process is reversible if the system and its surroundings can both be returned to their exact starting states, leaving no change anywhere. Nothing may be left behind: no warm spot on the cylinder, no stirred-up oil, no worn bearing.
Two conditions must hold at the same time.

items: Quasi-static: at every instant the driving force exceeds the resisting force by only an infinitesimal amount. The piston moves because the gas pressure is p + dp, not p + 2 bar. Heat flows because the gas sits at T + dT, not at T + 200 K.
No dissipative effect: no friction, no viscosity, no electrical resistance, no plastic deformation, no mixing of two different fluids.

blocks.text: The first condition removes finite gradients inside and across the boundary. The second rules out dissipative effects. A process is reversible only when the first holds and the second is met: no finite gradient anywhere inside or across the boundary, and no dissipation.

blocks.where: p is the pressure at the moving boundary in kPa, dV is the small volume change in m³, and W is the work in kJ. For a reversible path, p must be the gas pressure itself, uniform and known at every instant.

blocks.text: A reversible process creates no entropy, so it is the yardstick for everything else. The Carnot engine in 3.4 is only as good as this limit allows.
Every real process carries at least one of these. Each has the same two signatures: a finite gradient, or a one-way conversion of work into internal energy.

items: Friction in a pump or under a piston: shaft work heats the oil and the metal, and that heat never climbs back into the shaft by itself.
Unrestrained expansion: gas in one flask is connected to an evacuated flask. Nothing pushes back, so W = 0, yet the gas spreads over both flasks and cannot be gathered into one without spending work.
Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference: a hot vessel left in a room cools to room temperature. The same heat will not flow back up the same difference.
Mixing of two streams: hot and cold water joining in a shower line. Separating them again needs a heat pump and work.
Current through a resistance: all the electrical work becomes heat in the wire.
Plastic deformation: bending a steel rod past its yield point leaves it permanently bent and slightly warm.

blocks.text: Entropy (see 3.7) and the Clausius inequality (see 3.6) turn these signatures into a number.

Internal reversibility concerns only what happens inside the boundary: the gas has no pressure gradient, no temperature gradient and no internal friction, so at every instant it is uniform and in equilibrium.

External reversibility concerns the link with the surroundings: heat crosses only to a reservoir at the same temperature, and work is delivered to a load that is raised with no outside friction. A process may be internally reversible and externally irreversible. Standard texts define a reversible (totally reversible) process as one that is both internally and externally reversible. Many numerical problems only need internal reversibility, so check whether the surroundings are also idealised before assuming total reversibility.

No real process is reversible. We draw the reversible path the way a mathematician draws a smooth curve through measured points: it gives the best number possible, and the difference from reality is lost work, priced as exergy in Unit 4.
Slowness alone does not buy reversibility. A piston pushed very slowly against dry friction is quasi-static and still irreversible, because heat keeps appearing in the cylinder.

figure.caption: The smooth curve is the reversible path p = mRT/V; the stepped path drops pressure in jumps at constant volume and lies below the curve, so it encloses less area and delivers less work for the same volumes.

spec.aria: A smooth isothermal curve and a staircase of finite pressure steps between the same two volumes, the staircase lying below the curve and enclosing less area.

examples.question: 0.5 kg of air at 300 K expands at constant temperature from 0.2 m³ to 0.4 m³. Take R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). (a) Find the work delivered if the expansion is reversible and isothermal. (b) The same air is instead allowed to expand freely into an evacuated flask until it occupies 0.4 m³. Find the work delivered and the work lost.
steps: Data: m = 0.5 kg, T = 300 K, v₁ = 0.2 m³, v₂ = 0.4 m³, R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K).
For an ideal gas at constant temperature, p V = m R T, so p = m R T / V.
Reversible work: W_rev = ∫ p dV = m R T ∫ dV/V = m R T ln(v₂/v₁).
Free expansion: the gas pushes against nothing, so W = 0 kJ.

Work lost = 29.84 − 0 = 29.84 kJ. For an ideal gas in free expansion the temperature does not change and no heat is absorbed, so no energy is destroyed; what is lost is the 29.84 kJ of work that the reversible path could have delivered. That lost work equals T₀ × entropy generated = 300 × 0.0995 ≈ 29.84 kJ.
examples.answer: The reversible isothermal expansion delivers W_rev = 29.84 kJ; the free expansion delivers W = 0 kJ and loses all 29.84 kJ of possible work.
examples.check:
import math
m = 0.5
R = 0.287
T = 300
v1 = 0.2
v2 = 0.4
W_rev = m*R*T*math.log(v2/v1)
W_free = 0.0
lost = W_rev - W_free
print(round(W_rev, 2))
print(round(W_free, 2))
print(round(lost, 2))

traps: Quasi-static is necessary but not sufficient. A slow process with friction, or with a finite temperature difference across the wall, is still irreversible.
Reversible gives maximum work out of an expansion and minimum work into a compression. Do not apply the maximum rule to a compressor.
Free expansion gives W = 0 but is not reversible. For an ideal gas in an insulated flask the temperature also stays the same, which fools students into calling it isothermal and reversible.
Internally reversible is weaker than reversible. The boundary may still lose work to outside friction.
The entropy of the system may fall in an irreversible process, as when a hot block cools. The second law is applied to system plus surroundings together.

quiz.a: A process in which both the system and the surroundings can be restored exactly to their initial states, leaving no net change anywhere.
Friction, unrestrained or free expansion, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, mixing of two different fluids. (Electrical resistance and plastic deformation are also correct.)

quiz.q: Why does heat flow across a finite temperature difference make a process irreversible?
quiz.a: The flow needs a finite gradient, and once the heat has moved down the gradient it will not return up the same gradient without work from outside. A finite gradient is a signature of irreversibility.

quiz.q: Distinguish internal reversibility from external reversibility.
quiz.a: Internal reversibility means no gradients or friction inside the boundary, so the system is uniform at every instant. External reversibility means the interaction with the surroundings is also free of finite differences and dissipation, such as heat exchange with a reservoir at the same temperature.

quiz.q: 0.2 kg of nitrogen at 400 K expands reversibly and isothermally from 0.1 m³ to 0.3 m³. Take R = 0.2968 kJ/(kg·K). Find the work delivered.
A gas is compressed quasi-statically in a cylinder whose piston rubs on a dry guide. Is the process reversible? Compare the actual work input with the reversible work input.
quiz.a: Not reversible. Quasi-static only removes pressure gradients; the rubbing converts work into heat inside the cylinder and cannot be undone. The actual work input is larger than the reversible work input, because the reversible value is the minimum for a given change of state.

quiz.q: Air expands freely in an insulated flask: Q = 0 and W = 0, yet the process is irreversible. Explain.
quiz.a: The first law is satisfied because internal energy, and so temperature, does not change for an ideal gas. The second law is not satisfied for a reverse path: the gas would have to gather itself into one flask with no work input, which never happens. The irreversibility lies in the unrestrained expansion, and the entropy of the gas rises.

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant design the reversible path is the benchmark, and the shortfall is called exergy destruction; a steam turbine or a heat exchanger is judged by how close it comes. Second law efficiency compares a real device with that reversible best, and entropy generation computed from measured inlet and outlet states tells an engineer which unit to fix first. Search for exergy analysis, entropy generation minimisation, or pinch analysis for heat exchanger networks to go further.
